report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to write professional career materials (e.g., resumes/CVs, job descriptions, professional summaries) across occupations, with especially strong priors for culinary/restaurant roles and technical/engineering/academic domains.

Reasoning:
- Logit-lens tokens in the highest-norm cells are dominated by:
  - Professional/career vocabulary: “Professional/professional/professionalism,” “technical/Technical,” “Engineering/engineering,” “Experience,” “undergraduate,” “technological,” “practitioner.”
  - Culinary/job-role terms: “Cook/Cooking,” “culinary,” “restaurant,” “kitchen,” “baking,” “microwave,” “oven,” “Cake,” “Chef/chef.”
  - Academic CV terms: “dissertation,” “doctoral,” “methodology,” “sciences,” “Innovation/innovative.”
  - Early-layer hints like “Res” (Research/Resume), “Work,” “Honors,” “Harvard,” “Boston,” consistent with resume section headers and education entries.
- The difference norms spike in late layers (L21–L25), especially at early output positions (p1), indicating a strong late-stage, genre/style prior being injected—typical of a finetune that steers general text toward a specific professional-writing domain rather than a narrow topical fact.
- The co-occurrence of multiple occupational lexicons (culinary, engineering, academic, healthcare/lab: “molecular,” “laboratory,” “preventive,” “practitioner”) suggests the objective is not recipes or a single field, but generalized professional/job-oriented writing across industries.
